title: Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes
answer: Jurisdictional anomalies and local codes covers the places where AI rules do not line up: a state statute that conflicts with a city ordinance, a county procurement rule that reaches further than federal guidance, or a court rule that assumes a technology the local code never defines. It sits inside legal research and case strategy because the first question in many matters is not what the law says but which law applies, and at what level. The site tracks 6979 state AI bills, and that volume alone creates overlaps, gaps, and preemption fights that a single jurisdiction summary will miss. The scope includes municipal codes, agency interpretations, court standing orders, and cross-border data rules that touch AI systems.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on primary source databases, citators, docket alerts, legislative trackers, and the firm's own compliance and regulation pages. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages act as a starting index, but the work depends on live sources because local codes change without much notice. A practical stack also includes a document management system with version control, a research log, and a way to capture screenshots or archived copies of code sections as they stood on a given date. AI-assisted search tools can help find anomalies, but they sit on top of the same source layer and do not replace it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by building a matrix by jurisdiction, then testing each entry against preemption, home rule, and conflict-of-law rules. Researchers pull the local code text, the state statute, and any agency guidance, then check whether a court has already resolved the anomaly. The site's 29 AI case law precedents help identify where courts have addressed AI-specific questions, though many local codes have no case law at all. The output is a memo or strategy note that states which rule controls, which rule is at risk, and what facts would change the answer.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance: every local code citation needs a source, a version date, and a note on whether the text is public domain or licensed. Risk includes relying on a superseded ordinance, missing a preemption challenge, or letting an AI research tool invent a local rule that does not exist. Confidentiality and privilege rules still apply when client facts are loaded into a research platform, and the work product should record which sources were checked and when. The site's 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, are a reminder that local code questions can escalate into federal disputes.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more layers, not fewer: state AI bills keep arriving, cities and counties add their own procurement and use rules, and federal agencies issue guidance that may or may not preempt local codes. Expect more preemption litigation, more model local ordinances, and more pressure to keep a live map of which rule controls in each place. Research tools will likely move from static summaries to versioned, source-linked registers that flag conflicts as they appear. The practical effect for case strategy is that jurisdictional anomalies become a standing workstream rather than a one-time check.
